title: Semantic Framing and User Engagement: Evidence from Large-Scale Headline Experiments Using Language Model Embeddings
affiliations: and Michigan State University

detail.title: Semantic Framing and User Engagement: Evidence from Large-Scale Headline Experiments Using Language Model Embeddings
detail.abstract: This study examines how semantic framing shapes online engagement by connecting psychologically interpretable traits with large language model (LLM) embeddings. Using more than 40,000 randomized Upworthy headline experiments, within-test fixed-effects regressions show that curiosity, communication clarity, creativity, and social or cultural cues increase click-through rates (CTR), whereas cognitive complexity and prosocial or moral framing reduce them. To evaluate predictive value, we test whether trait-based models identify the winning headline within each experiment. Twelve traits derived from pretrained models reach a 30.8% win rate, and LoRA-adapted embeddings improve this to 36.1%. Ranking metrics such as Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG) and CTR regret similarly show that LoRA-enhanced semantic representations better capture user preferences. Overall, the findings demonstrate that semantic framing reliably influences audience attention and that combining interpretable psychological dimensions with LLM-based embeddings provides a scalable, theory-driven approach for modeling engagement in digital media.

title: Does political control shape DEI scores for nursing education institutions within the USA?: A new digital method for measuring institutional engagement with Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) in nursing
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Does political control shape DEI scores for nursing education institutions within the USA?: A new digital method for measuring institutional engagement with Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) in nursing
detail.abstract: Background: Diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) in nursing refers to an organization's explicit commitment to principles and practices that treat all employees and patients equally by recognizing diversity and upholding dignity and human rights. In recent years there has been an upsurge in “anti-DEI” political sentiment and legislation in the United States. This study develops a new digital method for measuring institutional engagement with Diversity, Equity and Inclusion. This can be used to assess the impact of state political control on the commitment of nursing education institutions to Diversity, Equity and Inclusion principles.Objective: To examine how the political climate and mode of funding relates to Diversity, Equity and Inclusion in nursing schools, using a web mining technique to examine the websites of nursing schools.Setting: The study examined websites of all colleges, schools and universities offering nursing qualifications in the USA.  Methods: Web mining was conducted for the years 2020-2024 using the Wayback Machine. Using code developed for this study, a web tool accessed a URL and then crawled the websites of 730 nursing education institutions using their landing page plus the first level of all linked pages. Nursing school web pages were compared with the Diversity, Equity and Inclusion policy of the American Association of Nursing Colleges (AACN) and the degree of alignment computed.Results: In 2024, the average Diversity, Equity and Inclusion score for institutions in Republican controlled states were higher than in Democrat controlled states, despite efforts in Republican controlled states to bring forward bills limiting Diversity, Equity and Inclusion programs within education institutions. All institutions recorded a higher average Diversity Equity and Inclusion score in 2024 than in 2020 and public universities saw the largest increase in the average Diversity, Equity and inclusion score.Conclusions: The study provides healthcare professionals, policymakers and researchers a new digital method for measuring institutional engagement with Diversity, Equity and Inclusion. It provides a data source to support policy research by helping to investigate whether anti-Diversity, Equity and Inclusion legislation is impacting upon Diversity, Equity and Inclusion in nursing education institutions. The strongest evidence of an impact of different political ideologies upon the public expression of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion by nursing education institutions is in those states where neither political party has overall political control.

title:
AI, Children’s Rights, & Wellbeing: Transnational Frameworks
Mapping 13 Frameworks at the Intersections of Data-Intensive Technologies, Children’s Rights, and Wellbeing
affiliations: The Alan Turing Institute, The Alan Turing Institute, University of Edinburgh, The Alan Turing Institute and The Alan Turing Institute

detail.title:
AI, Children’s Rights, & Wellbeing: Transnational Frameworks
Mapping 13 Frameworks at the Intersections of Data-Intensive Technologies, Children’s Rights, and Wellbeing
detail.abstract:
As data-intensive technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), become more commonplace, children are being impacted from birth and over the course of their lives. However, research is currently scarce when considering a comparative view of existing frameworks relating to AI, children’s rights, and wellbeing. Our research aims to fill this gap by exploring the emerging international governance landscape in this context, emphasising transnational frameworks to offer a comprehensive view of this landscape.

Our report explores the international and global reach of AI to assess how children are directly and indirectly affected by AI. First, we introduce a glossary of key terms, followed by our methodology outlining the frameworks reviewed and key themes. These themes encompass children’s rights, children’s wellbeing, and child-centred recommendations and policies. We then present two heatmaps which assesses the key themes across 13 transnational frameworks and the extent to which they address specific considerations within these themes. These include integrating children’s rights, considering children’s wellbeing and sociotechnical factors, involving children’s voices, and addressing both opportunities and risks related to AI. Finally, we conclude with a brief discussion and point to areas for future research.

Our research aims to provide insights for policymakers, researchers, public sector stakeholders, and civil society to understand the evolving landscape of AI frameworks concerning children’s rights and wellbeing on a global scale. The main findings of our analysis focus on the key areas of children’s rights, children’s wellbeing, and child-centred recommendation and policies.

title: Statistical Foundations of Conformal Prediction
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: Statistical Foundations of Conformal Prediction
detail.abstract: Conformal prediction is conventionally presented as a model-free, distribution-free mechanism for constructing finite-sample valid prediction sets. We develop a comprehensive estimation-theoretic foundation revealing conformal methods as structured estimators of calibration functionals. Working in nonparametric i.i.d. and time-series models, we identify residual-based limit functionals, derive asymptotic linear representations with explicit influence functions, and prove semiparametric inefficiency in heteroskedastic settings with quantified efficiency loss. We introduce coverage operators Γ P,G and prove conformal calibration estimates Γ-1 P,G (1-α) under exchangeability. We characterize non-stationary failure modes and prove an impossibility theorem for universal coverage under arbitrary distributional shifts. Adaptive conformal inference (ACI) and AgACI are reinterpreted as stochastic approximation algorithms tracking time-varying calibration maps. We embed conformal prediction in Bayesian frameworks via conformal-Bayesian operators achieving frequentist validity regardless of prior misspecification. Complete proofs are provided for all results.

title: Learning Heterogeneity from Unstructured Data: An Application to Chatbot Personalization
affiliations: University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management and University of Pennsylvania - Marketing Department

detail.title: Learning Heterogeneity from Unstructured Data: An Application to Chatbot Personalization
detail.abstract: Understanding and leveraging individual customer heterogeneity is fundamental to effective marketing personalization, yet little work has examined how unstructured data describing individual consumers can predict their preferences. We develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework that maps consumer-generated unstructured data, represented as embeddings, to heterogeneous preference parameters. Our approach generalizes the classic multilevel model to allow for neural networks to parameterize the link from customer data to model parameters. We estimate the model using amortized variational inference, enabling efficient, real-time targeting and preference learning. The Bayesian formulation naturally accommodates both observed heterogeneity (via embeddings) and unobserved heterogeneity (via posterior updating). We apply our method to chatbot personalization, where a user's initial query is mapped to expected stylistic preferences in the response. Our results demonstrate that substantial heterogeneity in style preferences can be predicted from query content alone, but incorporating choice data to uncover unobserved heterogeneity significantly improves prediction. Moreover, such improvements are systematic: specific attributes of conversations, and specific types of prompts benefit more from eliciting choice data than others, suggesting a role for adaptivity in how data are gathered. Our framework enables scalable chatbot personalization through prompt modifications without requiring model retraining. Beyond this application, our framework demonstrates how consumer-side unstructured data can enhance preference measurement in choice models, with applications extending to any setting where consumer-generated content can inform personalization strategies.

title: How Political Identity Shapes Preference for Extraordinary Brand Experiences
affiliations: , University of Texas at San Antonio, Catholic University of Portugal and Rice University

detail.title: How Political Identity Shapes Preference for Extraordinary Brand Experiences

keywords: Primal World Beliefs that the World Is Worth Exploring

detail.abstract: This article examines the effect of political identity on preference for extraordinary (vs. ordinary) brand experiences. It documents systematic and robust differences in preference for extraordinary experiences between liberals and conservatives. This differential preference systematically manifests across (1) five secondary studies (with a composite sample of more than 3 million observations, including 273,523 individuals, 51 brands, and 83 product categories) that identify the effect of political identity on preference for extraordinary experiences and their downstream consequences, and (2) five primary studies (with a composite sample size of 2,912) that examine the underlying mechanism rooted in the different world beliefs of liberals and conservatives. While liberals' stronger belief that the world is worth exploring mediates their preference for extraordinary experiences, conservatives' stronger belief that the world is dangerous hinders such exploratory tendency. These findings offer important contributions to the political identity literature and to the understanding of the choices and motivations of liberals. They also offer valuable insights to practitioners about how brands can position themselves for different customer segments based on their political identity.

title: Behavioural Science, Health Policy, and Education: A Multi-Level Analysis of Locker Installation in Indian Schools with Evidence-Informed Recommendations
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Behavioural Science, Health Policy, and Education: A Multi-Level Analysis of Locker Installation in Indian Schools with Evidence-Informed Recommendations
detail.abstract: Heavy school bags pose significant but preventable risks to children’s physical and psychological health, particularly in countries such as India where infrastructural limitations, socio-cultural norms, and policy gaps intersect. This paper provides a multi-level policy and behavioural analysis of locker installation in Indian schools, drawing on international guidelines, national education and health policies, and evidence-based behavioural science. Using the Socio-Ecological Model and the Health Belief Model, the analysis maps how individual, interpersonal, institutional, community, and policy-level factors shape health behaviours and implementation outcomes. A biopsychosocial lens is used to examine musculoskeletal strain, hygiene concerns, anxiety, social dynamics, and structural inequalities linked to current school bag practices. Findings indicate that existing policy measures – including the National Education Policy (2020), the Policy on School Bag (2020), and the School Health Programme under Ayushman Bharat – insufficiently address the long-term physical burden of heavy bags or the need for secure and accessible storage within schools. Cultural beliefs associating heavy bags with discipline, infrastructural barriers in densely populated or low-resource schools, and limited policy recognition of non-disability health concerns further constrain progress. The paper offers evidence-informed recommendations such as ergonomic locker design, broader vulnerability criteria, interdisciplinary stakeholder collaboration, psychoeducational interventions, and policy revision grounded in the Progressive Realisation Principle. Integrating lockers within a health-promoting schools framework can enhance students’ physical and psychological well-being while advancing India’s goals for equitable, inclusive, and child-centred education.

title: HRM and Line Managers, the Recipe of Organizational Success
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: HRM and Line Managers, the Recipe of Organizational Success
detail.abstract: Finding a roadmap for the relation between Human resources management (HRM) unit and line managers in other units of an organization is a goal that need to be in the center of interest. This will eliminate the overlap between both units roles, which will make any organization more effective and more successful. However, HRM unit becomes crucial in any organization because HRM practices are vital for the success of any organization. Nevertheless, the question remains, can this unit run all human resources in the organization? Do HRM units hear and understand the claim of other units? On the other hand, line managers have crucial role for the success and survival of any organization. Since they have specific roles to conduct in their organization. Then, another question arises, can they do their job alone? Are they delivering their  HRM role? Accordingly, an organization must acquire  HRM staff,  who can hear, understand, and support, and  be the guidance idol for every and each line manager. This research is designed as qualitative study. A questionnaire was designed with open question to collect primary data from the community related to hiring practices in the civil sector of Palestine. The tool was conducted through google forms to ensure proper timing of responses and proper collection for data. Moreover, answers were categorized and analyzed, the SPSS program was used to investigate the trends. The population was the supervisory-positions employees who work at Ministry Of Education of Palestine (MoE). 160 employees send recommendations that are related to hiring practices, where all the recommendations hovered around the need to improve hiring practices, the quality of Employment policies, the strength and weakness of recruitment and selection practices.

title: Safety, Growth, and the Bureaucratic Trade-off: Evidence from Municipal Planning in China
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Shanghai University of Finance and Economics and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Safety, Growth, and the Bureaucratic Trade-off: Evidence from Municipal Planning in China
detail.abstract: How do local governments recalibrate policy priorities after public safety shocks? Using 5,539 government work reports from Chinese cities (2003-2022), this study examines how industrial accidents reshape planning discourse, safety outcomes, and economic performance. We construct a text-based measure of "work safety" emphasis to quantify bureaucratic attention in formal planning documents. Each additional industrial accident increases safety-related content by 0.16 percentage points, with stronger effects in prospective sections. Greater emphasis on safety predicts fewer industrial accidents and fatalities in subsequent years, suggesting that official discourse functions as a coordination and commitment mechanism within local administrations. Yet, this shift entails economic costs: a one-percentage point increase in safety salience corresponds to a 0.29 percentage point decline in GDP growth and lower growth and investment targets. These results show that local governments dynamically rebalance rhetoric and policy, trading short-term growth for risk mitigation and institutional learning.

title: Geopolitics Beyond Identity: Ukraine and the Structural Trap of Great-Power Competition
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Geopolitics Beyond Identity: Ukraine and the Structural Trap of Great-Power Competition

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, financial, or institutional relationships that could be perceived as influencing the research. All analyses and conclusions were developed independently and without external pressure or involvement.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or experimental procedures. It is a theoretical and analytical work based entirely on public-domain sources and academic literature; therefore, formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently and self-supported by the author as part of ongoing academic work on the Third Generation in International Relations.

detail.abstract: This essay develops an exchange initiated by Dr Andreas Umland concerning whether a Russian victory in Ukraine would incentivise smaller non-nuclear states to pursue weapons of mass destruction. Walter Fiori expanded the discussion by raising fundamental questions about the alleged civilisational unity between Russians and Ukrainians, unresolved minority rights in Donbass, the strategic objectives of Western involvement, and the deeper geopolitical architecture governing the war. Integrating classical realism, structural theories of international politics, and the emergent framework of Third-Generation International Relations (IR3), this paper contends that identity is not a driver of state behaviour; that Ukraine’s misfortune derives from its placement at the intersection of rival great-power spheres; that Western strategy exploited Ukraine as an instrument without providing a realistic prospect for victory; and that failure to acknowledge these structural constraints is both intellectually misleading and ethically untenable.

title: The Trump Effect: An Event Study of Asymmetric Bitcoin Market Responses to Political News
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: The Trump Effect: An Event Study of Asymmetric Bitcoin Market Responses to Political News
detail.abstract: This study empirically tests economist Paul Krugman's thesis that Bitcoin has become a "Trump trade," driven by expectations of political favoritism rather than monetary fundamentals. Using daily returns data from January 2024 through November 2025, I employ a three-stage econometric approach combining correlation analysis, factor regression, and market-adjusted event studies. Findings reveal that daily political sentiment, measured by changes in Donald Trump's approval ratings, has no continuous predictive power over Bitcoin returns (r = .04). Bitcoin instead exhibits characteristics of a high-beta risk asset, with returns predominantly driven by equity market movements (β = 0.97, p < .001). The average abnormal return across 30 key political and macroeconomic events is statistically significant at the 10% level (p = .079). However, this average masks substantial heterogeneity; a small subset of uncertainty-resolving events generated disproportionately large returns, particularly the November 15, 2024 Trump-industry meeting (+5.63%) and Election Day 2024 (+1.07%). These findings suggest Bitcoin responds not to political drama itself, but to rare moments when policy outcomes materially alter regulatory expectations. This pattern challenges the semi-strong form of market efficiency and validates a nuanced Trump trade thesis: Bitcoin's value depends on political patronage, but this dependence manifests episodically at critical junctures rather than continuously.

title: Divide and Conquer: Bargaining Scope and the Distribution of Rents
affiliations: University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy and University of Chicago - Department of Economics

detail.title: Divide and Conquer: Bargaining Scope and the Distribution of Rents
detail.abstract: This paper studies how legal firm boundaries that constrain the scope of collective bargaining affect wages, rent sharing, and productivity. We analyze a 2014 Chilean labor-code reform that prevented corporations from fragmenting their workforce into smaller legal entities, thereby expanding the potential size of bargaining units. Using population-wide matched employer-employee administrative data and a dynamic difference-indifferences design with same-industry controls, we find that average annual earnings rose by 4.7%, bottom-decile wages by 10%, and within-firm wage dispersion (standard deviation) by $520-$710 (USD), corresponding to 6-9% of its pre-reform level. Employment and firm profits did not change, while value added per worker increased. Effects are strongest in initially smaller businesses and in multi-establishment groups with co-located units, consistent with coordination-cost frictions. We develop an extensive-form model in which management chooses whether to fragment or consolidate its business, and payoffs are determined by subsequent bargaining with workers. Under consolidation, workers can form an encompassing union that worsens management's outside option during a strike, while the firm internalizes cross-unit complementarities in production. The model predicts higher worker effort, wages, and wage dispersion under consolidation, matching our empirical results and rationalizing their heterogeneity. Overall, the analysis shows that expanding bargaining-unit scope can be efficiency-consistent: coordination gains offset rent reallocation, allowing efficiency and equity to coexist within firms.

title: Learning to Prompt: Human Adaptation in Production with Generative AI
affiliations: University of Toronto, Toronto, Canada

detail.title: Learning to Prompt: Human Adaptation in Production with Generative AI
detail.abstract: What is the role of human input in AI-assisted production? Humans interact with generative AI through combinations of words called prompts. A key feature of human input is adaptation: users dynamically modify their prompts based on their understanding of AI. I empirically investigate two types of adaptation: (1) adaptation to new AI versions, referring to how people change their prompts in response to AI upgrades; (2) adaptation to outputs from previous prompts, referring to how people adjust their prompts iteratively to converge on desired outcomes. I study this adaptation using prompt-level data from Midjourney, a leading AI image generator. First, users adapt to AI upgrades by writing different words in their prompts. By submitting prompts written for the old version to the new AI and vice versa, I decompose the output shifts as arising from prompt changes (73%), AI changes (20%), and an AI-human cross effect (7%), implying complementarity between AI and human inputs. Second, prompts evolve within the creative process of an artwork. I estimate a structural model of the creative process using the sequential search framework. Counterfactual shows that without human adaptation, users need three times more prompts to achieve data-observed results. Both results highlight the importance of human judgment and adaptation in the creative process.

title: Monetary Policy and Volatility
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: Monetary Policy and Volatility
detail.abstract: This paper provides empirical evidence that the effectiveness of monetary policy transmission depends negatively on volatility and develops a general equilibrium model to quantify this relationship. In the cross section, firms with higher return volatility exhibit weaker responses to monetary policy shocks in both capital investment and equity prices. Similarly, in the time series, the stock market and aggregate investment are less responsive to monetary policy shocks when aggregate volatility is high. I develop a two-sector general equilibrium model with price rigidity and endogenous growth to quantify the relationship between volatility and the strength of monetary policy transmission.

title: Operationalizing Ummatic Soft Power: Criteria for Effective Collaboratives
affiliations: International University of Sarajevo

detail.title: Operationalizing Ummatic Soft Power: Criteria for Effective Collaboratives
detail.abstract: Building on a previous paper that conceptualized ummatic soft power and identified its domains, this paper focuses on its operationalization through collaboratives: decentralized, value-driven networks designed to unite the Umma towards common goals. It introduces six foundational criteria for the effective functioning of these collaboratives: ummatic orientation, cooperation, decentralization, representation of the Umma's diversity, managing differences, and selfcorrection. These criteria ensure that collaboratives remain aligned with the broader civilizational vision of the Umma, fostering cooperation across national and ideological boundaries. The paper emphasizes the importance of decentralization to avoid the risks of cooptation and centralization, while also stressing the need for effective management of differences within diverse groups within the Umma. It advocates for self-correction mechanisms to maintain integrity and adapt to changing circumstances. The paper concludes with a call for an independent ratings organization to audit and ensure transparency, accountability, and alignment with Islamic principles, thereby reinforcing the collaboratives' credibility and fostering long-term sustainability for the collective good of the Umma.

title: A Model of Fed Information Effect
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison and University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: A Model of Fed Information Effect
detail.abstract: A significant fraction of measured surprise central bank interest rate hikes is associated with simultaneous stock market run-ups and upward revisions in economic growth forecasts. This evidence is often interpreted as contradicting the standard New Keynesian transmission mechanism and as indicating that the Fed possesses superior information about economic fundamentals. We present a New Keynesian model in which investors are uncertain about the Fed's long-run monetary policy objectives and learn from observed Fed actions. Our model does not assume that the Fed has superior information, but it nonetheless generates a "Fed information effect," that is, a positive co-movement between interest rate surprises, revisions in expected growth, and stock returns as an equilibrium outcome. We show that the key predictions of our model are consistent with empirical evidence on asset market responses to measured Fed information shocks.

title: America Invents Act and Innovation Acquisition: A Race to Acquire Patents?
affiliations: Sabanci University, Istanbul Bilgi University and Sabanci University

detail.title: America Invents Act and Innovation Acquisition: A Race to Acquire Patents?
detail.abstract: This study examines how America Invents Act (AIA), particularly its shift from a "first-to-invent" to a "first-inventor-to-file" priority rule, affects innovation acquisition. Using the Act as a quasi-natural experiment, we find innovative firms became more likely acquisition targets post-AIA. This increased demand is further evidenced by more frequent contested bids, longer deal completions, and higher bid premiums for innovative targets during that time. Acquirers of these targets subsequently reduced their own patenting, indicating a substitution effect between internal and external innovation. The findings reveal a more competitive and less cooperative patenting environment post-AIA, forcing firms to exit the market or acquire innovation through M&As.

title: Digital Transformation of Public Financial Management in Ghana and Developing Economies: A Systematic Review of Accountability, Transparency, and Efficiency
affiliations: Ministry of Finance and Economic Planning and Transilvania University of Brasov

detail.title: Digital Transformation of Public Financial Management in Ghana and Developing Economies: A Systematic Review of Accountability, Transparency, and Efficiency

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors report there are no competing interests to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This systematic review rigorously assesses the digitisation of Public Financial Management (PFM) in Ghana and similar developing economies, examining how major digital tools such as IFMIS, e-procurement, and digital payment platforms promote accountability, transparency, and fiscal discipline. It synthesises empirical evidence and theoretical insights from studies published between 2013 and 2025 and aims to (1) analyze bibliometric trends in digital PFM research, (2) evaluate PFM effectiveness and governance by considering legal frameworks, audit quality, and digital technologies on transparency and local government performance, (3) assess implementation barriers and the quality of evidence by identifying structural challenges and evaluating methodological rigor, (4) examine theoretical and comparative perspectives to synthesize dominant frameworks and compare digital interventions, and (5) develop a synthesis framework that maps the pathways from digital interventions through governance factors to institutional outcomes. Methodology: Following the PRISMA 2020 framework, the study collates empirical findings and theoretical insights from peer-reviewed literature published between 2013 and 2025 using Python (v3.11) supplemented by manual data extraction. The synthesis organizes evidence to examine the relationship between technology adoption and institutional outcomes. Findings: The analysis shows that digital PFM solutions markedly strengthen budget credibility, streamline procurement, and widen the tax base through real-time revenue monitoring. However, their effectiveness varies. While a distinct "transparency dividend" emerges, achieving Value for Money (VFM) is often limited by infrastructure gaps, weak regulatory adherence, and organisational pushback. Crucially, the review demonstrates that technology is most successful when supported by solid internal audit systems, independent auditor-client links, and strong political commitment. Originality: Diverging from earlier work that treated digitisation in isolation, this review underscores the moderating influence of "soft" governance elements-such as ethical leadership and normative legal frameworks-on unlocking the benefits of "hard" digital infrastructure. Practical implications: The study concludes that digitisation alone does not guarantee PFM reform. Policymakers should adopt a comprehensive strategy that couples digital infrastructure investment with institutional capacity building and rigid legal enforcement. Future research ought to focus on longitudinal designs to trace causal pathways between digital adoption and reduced fiscal waste.

title: Intangible Intensity
affiliations: UCLA Anderson School of Management, University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management, University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business and

detail.title: Intangible Intensity
detail.abstract: We develop a text-based measure of intangible investment intensity derived from firms' 10-K filings. Our approach further classifies disclosure text into knowledge, customer, and organization capital. Firms with high intangible intensity are smaller, younger, and invest heavily in R&D, SG&A, and human capital, while the three subcomponents map cleanly to distinct economic firm types. Intangible intensity contains information about future profitability that is not captured by standard accounting measures. Managerial language thus embeds forward-looking signals about intangible investment that accounting data obscure.

title: Existential Risk and Axiomatic Rationality: Lexical Convergence within Expected Utility Theory
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Existential Risk and Axiomatic Rationality: Lexical Convergence within Expected Utility Theory
detail.abstract: Expected Utility Theory is widely held to fail when outcomes carry infinite value-from Pascal's Wager to existential risks-thus muting rational decision theory's role in urgent debates such as AI misalignment and climate tipping points. We prove this collapse is a misapplication, not a flaw. Under von Neumann-Morgenstern normalization, a single infinite outcome triggers lawful compression: all finite utilities collapse into a vanishing band, preserving all axioms while reducing rational choice to a derived two-layer lexicographic rule: first, minimize catastrophe probability, and second, as a tie-breaker, maximize finite-outcome utility. A Lexical Convergence Theorem shows that Rank-Dependent Utility, Cumulative Prospect Theory, Choquet Expected Utility, maximin, and discounted EUT all converge point-wise to this two-layer lexicographic rule on finite menus; Allais anomalies vanish within the ε-band. An exhaustive structural taxonomy closes the loop on infinity in decision theory: as concavity resolves St. Petersburg (series-based infinity), compression-for the first time-rigorously resolves Pascal's Wager and existential risks (lexical infinity class). The result is not optional but authoritative: once an outcome permanently forecloses humanity's unbounded future, rationality demands p ∞ → 0. For AI alignment and climate tipping, as exemples, no finite benefit compensates for positive existential risk.

title: The Colocation Friction: Dual-Earner Job Search, Migration, and Labor Market Outcomes
affiliations: Boston College and Boston College

detail.title: The Colocation Friction: Dual-Earner Job Search, Migration, and Labor Market Outcomes
detail.abstract: We develop a spatial directed search model to study job search and migration among dual-earner households. Using the model, we decompose observed gender gaps into exogenous gender differences, which are amplified by a "colocation friction" that is unique to dual-earner households. Estimated for the U.S. labor market, the colocation friction reduces women's long-term migration gains by 19% and discourages mobility, particularly among "power couples". The rise of remote work mitigates this friction, cutting average earnings losses by up to 50%.

title: Responsible Mutual Fund Management
affiliations: and Universidad Europea de Madrid

detail.title: Responsible Mutual Fund Management
detail.abstract: Data provided by both national and international institutions reveal the growing interest that individual investors are showing towards sustainable and responsible investment (SRI) funds. While they desire positive returns, these investors expect mutual funds to invest in assets that meet environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria. These criteria impose a clear limitation on the strategies that SRI fund managers can apply. Does the dual financial and ethical purpose imply a differential behavior on the part of SRI fund managers? The main objective of this paper is to provide an economic and psychological perspective on SRI. We will analyze, through a literature review, whether there are differences in profitability between conventional mutual funds and SRI funds and examine the relationship between profitability and cash flow, as well as the existence of the disposition effect in SRI, in order to offer managers and potential investors a comprehensive view for their investment decision-making process.

title: Framing Allais: Is the Paradox Robust to the Pictorial Framing of Probabilities?
affiliations: Tor Vergata University of Rome and University of Insubria - Department of Economics

detail.title: Framing Allais: Is the Paradox Robust to the Pictorial Framing of Probabilities?
detail.abstract: The Allais paradox refers to a choice problem in which individuals face two pairs of lotteries, A-B and C-D, and typically prefer A to B and D to C, a choice pattern that violates Expected Utility theory. Prior theoretical and experimental work suggests that the AD pattern is sensitive to features of experimental design and that framing the probabilities of outcomes pictorially rather than numerically may reduce its incidence. We test this hypothesis in an online experiment (N=595) with three treatments. In Baseline, outcome probabilities are presented numerically as fractions. The two pictorial treatments are Pie, where probabilities are displayed using pie charts, and Grid, which represents probabilities through a grid of colored balls. Contrary to our expectations, we find that the frequency of the AD pattern is substantially the same across the three treatments, indicating that the Allais paradox is robust to the pictorial framing of lottery-outcome probabilities. We then discuss some implications of our findings.

title: Payment Methods and Market Feedback in Mergers and Acquisitions
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics, University of Macau, Faculty of Business Administration, University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management and

detail.title: Payment Methods and Market Feedback in Mergers and Acquisitions
detail.abstract: We document that M&A withdrawals are more sensitive to acquirers' announcement returns when the deal is financed entirely with cash, suggesting an intriguing interaction between payment methods and market feedback. Motivated by this evidence, we develop a model in which managers learn about deal synergies from post-announcement stock prices, with the payment method shaping the informativeness of this feedback. Our theory not only explains these differing feedback patterns but also yields unique predictions for how the choice of payment method depends on financial market characteristics. We test these predictions in a merger-arbitrageur setting and find supporting evidence.

reference: Working Paper CocciaLab n. 71/2025, pp. 1-36, CNR -- National Research Council of Italy
title: Optimal Rate of Foreign Direct Investment in Deglobalization Dynamics to Maximize Export and GDP Per Capita
affiliations: National Research Council of Italy (CNR)

detail.title: Optimal Rate of Foreign Direct Investment in Deglobalization Dynamics to Maximize Export and GDP Per Capita

publicationDetails.detailsText: Working Paper CocciaLab n. 71/2025, pp. 1-36, CNR -- National Research Council of Italy

detail.abstract: This study investigates the complex relationship between globalization, international trade, and wealth creation within the global political economy. While prevailing theories often associate higher levels of globalization with increased economic growth and export performance, this research challenges such assumptions by analyzing long-term data from 1971 to 2023. The findings reveal that elevated levels of globalization do not necessarily correlate with greater export volumes or higher GDP per capita. Instead, inconsistencies within the global system-exacerbated by geopolitical conflicts, economic shocks, and protectionist trade policies-can undermine the potential benefits of globalization. Drawing on interdisciplinary perspectives from political economy, international relations, and development studies, the analysis introduces the concept of a global optimal rate of foreign direct investment (FDI) net outflows (% of GDP). This threshold represents a critical point beyond which the positive effects of globalization on export and national wealth begin to diminish. The study suggests that exceeding this optimal rate may lead to systemic decline, characterized by reduced export capacity and stagnating GDP per capita across nations. These insights contribute to ongoing debates on the sustainability of current development models and the need for recalibrated economic policies. By identifying structural limits within globalization dynamics, the research offers a framework for policymakers to design more balanced and resilient strategies that align with the goals of inclusive growth and global equity. Ultimately, the study advocates for a rethinking of globalization not as an unbounded force, but as a process that requires careful governance, strategic investment flows, and coordinated international regulation to foster long-term prosperity.

title: From Hype to Grey Swans: Governing AI-Enabled Strategic Foresight

detail.title: From Hype to Grey Swans: Governing AI-Enabled Strategic Foresight
detail.abstract: A recent OECD-World Economic Forum report, AI in Strategic Foresight: Reshaping Anticipatory Governance, shows that many foresight practitioners already use AI tools for horizon scanning, clustering, and scenario development, while expressing serious concerns about hallucinations, bias, opacity, skill gaps, and uneven access, particularly in the public sector. This short paper argues that the binding constraint is no longer access to AI tools but the lack of disciplined, governed methods for integrating them into foresight. Building on Simpson (2025), it presents the Grey Swan / Archimedes framework as one such method. Grey Swan defines a rule-based evidence architecture (Tier 0-3), focuses attention on underpriced but structurally plausible "grey swan" disruptions, and links AI-assisted scanning and synthesis to a small set of public, measurable indicators and policy levers. AI is used for enforcement, logging, and narrative packaging; humans retain control over framing, thresholds, and value judgements. The paper positions Grey Swan as an immediately implementable template for AI-enabled anticipatory governance in middle-capacity states and organisations.

title: Remote and Hybrid Work and Productivity
affiliations: San Juan College

detail.title: Remote and Hybrid Work and Productivity
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of remote and hybrid work has become one of the most defining transformations in the labor market. What began as a temporary response to the COVID-19 pandemic has evolved into a long-term thing for how, when and where employees do their jobs. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), the share of employees working remotely increased in 2020 as businesses across the United States seek to protect worker's health while maintaining continuity of operations (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2021). This has messed up things within the workplace and it has caused reevaluations of the products, and organize cultural, and all employee's well-being.

title: Climate Policy and Structural Change: Evidence from Latin America
affiliations: Universidad de los Andes, Colombia - Department of Economics and Universidad de los Andes, Colombia

detail.title: Climate Policy and Structural Change: Evidence from Latin America
detail.abstract: We study how energy prices shape the decoupling in Latin America. We develop a multisector general equilibrium model to distinguish between two key channels: the technique effect (within-sector efficiency gains) and the composition effect (reallocation of economic activity). Using panel data for 21 Latin American countries from 1990 to 2021, we first employ a descriptive decomposition analysis and then test the model's predictions with a shift-share instrumental variable strategy. Our results reveal a clear dichotomy. Higher energy prices induce a persistent composition effect, shifting activity toward services. However, in manufacturing and transport—especially in developing and commodity-exporting economies—higher energy prices are linked to short-run increases in energy intensity, reflecting a perverse technique effect associated with scale expansion during booms. This tension highlights the need for policy approaches that address both structural and efficiency channels in resource-dependent economies.

title: Constructing Supply-Chain Input–Output Tables: Mapping Distribution Networks from Trade Margins
affiliations: International Institute of Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) and International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA)

detail.title: Constructing Supply-Chain Input–Output Tables: Mapping Distribution Networks from Trade Margins
detail.abstract: Input-output (IO) tables are essential for modeling supply chain networks. However, their accounting principles are inadequate for tracking product flows through supply and distribution channels. We propose a method to estimate the flows of products bought for resale and trace their pathway through trade intermediaries. Calibrated for Austria and applied to 21 countries using Eurostat data, the method yields modified "supply-chain" IO (SC-IO) tables, including supply, domestic use, and import tables. These SC-IO tables offer a more accurate representation of goods movement and the role of intermediaries in the economy. To demonstrate their relevance, we use a standard IO model to simulate the economic impacts of a hypothetical disruption to wholesale trade. Unlike conventional IO tables, the SC-IO framework captures propagation effects through the supply chain, leading to significantly higher estimates of indirect losses.

title: In-Silico Assessment of NDM-1 Inhibition and Its Relevance to Agricultural Productivity and Rural Healthcare Economics
affiliations: DY Patil School of Biotechnology and Bioinformatics

detail.title: In-Silico Assessment of NDM-1 Inhibition and Its Relevance to Agricultural Productivity and Rural Healthcare Economics
detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) threatens human health, livestock productivity, and food system stability across India. Central to this crisis is the New Delhi Metallo-β-Lactamase-1 (NDM-1), a di-zincdependent enzyme responsible for hydrolysing carbapenems, a critical class of last-line antibiotics. This study investigates the inhibitory potential of Captopril, a thiol-containing ligand with known zinc-chelation properties, using a comprehensive molecular docking workflow. The NDM-1 structure (PDB ID: 4HL2) was curated by retaining the biologically relevant chain and the two essential catalytic Zn²⁺ ions (Zn303 and Zn304), followed by ligand docking using AutoDock Vina. The highest-ranked pose exhibited a binding affinity of-4.7 kcal/mol, with the ligand positioned 2.61 Å from Zn303 and 3.58 Å from Zn304, distances consistent with plausible metal-mediated interaction. These findings underscore the viability of Captopril as a preliminary inhibitory scaffold and highlight the strategic utility of computational drug discovery in addressing AMR at low cost. The study further contextualizes these molecular insights within India's agricultural bioeconomy, where AMR imposes considerable burdens through reduced livestock productivity, elevated veterinary treatment costs, and increased rural healthcare expenditure.

title: Regulation versus Courts: The Equity Market's View
affiliations: Monash University, Australian National University (ANU) and Macquarie University, Macquarie Business School

detail.title: Regulation versus Courts: The Equity Market's View
detail.abstract: We examine how financial markets value regulation versus courts as mechanisms of enforcing property rights using the Supreme Court's 2024 reversal of Chevron deference, which ended four decades of judicial deference to regulatory agencies, as an exogenous event that shifted the institutional power from regulators to the judiciary. Using firm-level event studies, we find that the average market reaction was muted, but abnormal returns vary systematically across firms and industries. Heavily regulated and fragmented firms gained value, while small firms and those linked to congested or ideologically imbalanced courts lost value. These results suggest that investors view regulatory governance as costly but judicial governance as uncertain, implying that markets favor regulation's predictability over the decentralization and variability of court-based enforcement.

title: Extreme Trading Activity and Beta Pricing
affiliations: University of Bristol and University of Bristol

detail.title: Extreme Trading Activity and Beta Pricing
detail.abstract: Trading activity is typically very skewed in the cross-section of US stocks, with a small proportion exhibiting significantly more intense trading compared to most of their peers. We link this stylized fact with the pricing of market beta by showing that the relationship between CAPM beta and average return is linear and significantly positive when trading is less extreme in the right tail of the cross-sectional distribution. This effect is not driven by the positive beta-return relationship on announcement days documented in the literature and holds in a battery of robustness tests. We examine several potential economic mechanisms and find suggestive evidence that time-varying sentiment may help explain our results.

title: Regenerative Capital Theory: Beyond Debt, Equity, and Grants

detail.title: Regenerative Capital Theory: Beyond Debt, Equity, and Grants

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal, financial, or organizational interests that could be perceived as influencing the research presented in this paper. The study was conducted independently and without any external influence over the analysis, interpretation, or conclusions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or interventions requiring ethics approval. Therefore, no ethical review was necessary.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was entirely self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces Regenerative Capital Theory, a field-defining framework that expands the canonical capital taxonomy beyond debt, equity, and grants. Regenerative capital is defined by principal preservation, non-liability, soft-repayable structures, and multi-cycle value creation. These characteristics distinguish regenerative capital from all existing capital classes and allow it to generate positive-sum, non-extractive, system-level dynamics.

Building on the formal model of Perpetual Social Capital (PSC), the paper develops a general regenerative capital structure in which capital evolves recursively through recycling rates R∈[0,1]R \in [0,1]R∈[0,1], producing multi-cycle institutional strengthening, geometric social value accumulation, and system-level returns without extraction. The framework introduces concepts such as system IRR, total system value (TSV), and capital recursion, and demonstrates that even moderate recycling rates can outperform both grants and debt-financed models at the system level.

The paper contrasts regenerative and extractive capital systems, outlines the institutional design principles necessary for regenerative cycles (transparency, soft norms, governance alignment), and demonstrates applications in public finance, climate resilience, digital public goods, scientific infrastructure, and community systems. The work concludes by articulating a research agenda spanning behavioural dynamics, political economy, empirical evaluation, macro-fiscal integration, and global development. Regenerative Capital Theory establishes the conceptual and mathematical foundation for a new class of capital capable of compounding public value across time.

title: Do Advisors' Status and Identity Shape Adherence to Advice?
affiliations: Monash University, Monash University - Department of Economics, University of Gothenburg, Agricultural Economics, Social Sciences Division and GATE - CNRS

detail.title: Do Advisors' Status and Identity Shape Adherence to Advice?

declarations.funderStatement: iFREE CGIAR Initiatives Excellence in Agronomy

detail.abstract: This study examines whether adherence to advice depends on an advisor's identity and status beyond message content. Using a survey experiment with over 3000 farmers in India, we find that individuals are more likely to follow advice in a social dilemma game when it comes from high-status or in-group advisors, even when the advice diverges from prevailing norms. Admired role models can attenuate the influence of status and identity, though their beneficial effect is not universal. Our experimental findings align with evidence from an agricultural advisory program involving the same participant sample, highlighting the broader real-world relevance of these patterns.

title: Beyond Mammonism: Reconstructing the Boundaries of Rationality via Range-Clearing Theory — A Defense of Confucius and Socrates

detail.title: Beyond Mammonism: Reconstructing the Boundaries of Rationality via Range-Clearing Theory — A Defense of Confucius and Socrates
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the apparent antagonism between Classical economics and Behavioral economics is a charade, as both schools share a flawed "Mammonist" definition of rationality that equates utility maximization with monetary gain. By judging human behavior against this narrow benchmark, Behavioral economics acts merely as a pathologist for the Classical model, diagnosing "biases" where none exist. We propose a reconstruction of rationality based on the Austrian School's praxeological approach, augmented by a novel "Range-Clearing" framework. Through the historical examples of Confucius and Socrates, we demonstrate the existence of "Value Rationality," where actions such as sacrificing wealth for righteousness are not irrational deviations but purposeful behaviors consistent with subjective ends. Furthermore, we reinterpret four classic behavioral experiments—the Ultimatum Game, Framing Effect, Endowment Effect, and Anchoring Effect—through the lens of Range-Clearing Theory. We show that what appears to be "bias" is often a rational, energy-saving strategy for navigating fuzzy subjective value intervals under cognitive constraints. We conclude by calling for a return to the Misesian definition of rationality as purposeful action, rejecting the predictive hubris of mainstream models in favor of a deeper understanding of human choice.

title: Safe Haven No More? A Structural Break in the USD's Relative Risk Premium After the 2022 Russian Reserve Seizure

detail.title: Safe Haven No More? A Structural Break in the USD's Relative Risk Premium After the 2022 Russian Reserve Seizure
detail.abstract: This project investigates whether the global financial system experienced a fundamental change in the pricing of U.S. Treasury securities during periods of market stress following the 2022 seizure of Russian central bank reserves by the United States and its allies. Using high-frequency yield data from 20 countries and an event-study design centered on VIX spikes, the analysis uncovers a statistically and economically significant structural break in the USD relative risk premium-a break that reverses the traditional safe-haven behavior of U.S. long-term yields.

title: Shareholders' Protection Rights Perspectives from the New Ethiopian Company Law: Are There Improvements from the Old Law?
affiliations: University of East Anglia

detail.title: Shareholders' Protection Rights Perspectives from the New Ethiopian Company Law: Are There Improvements from the Old Law?
detail.abstract: This study critically evaluates the adequacy of shareholder protection rights under the New Company Law of Ethiopia 2021 in comparison with the relevant provisions of the 1960 Law to ascertain whether the New Law has adequately addressed and responded to the deficiencies of the Old Law in protecting shareholders' interests. The study highlights that, in comparison, the rules of shareholders' protection under the New Law are significantly improved, providing strong protection to the interests of shareholders in general and minority shareholders in particular.

title: The Essence of Money
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Essence of Money
detail.abstract: This book explores the essence of money through the lens of power theory of exchange. It offers a new understanding of the nature of money and its role in society. Based on an original mathematical model of exchange, which examines the mutual transfer of generalized power over objects by parties, the author formulates a power theory of money, according to which money is a measure and certification of power. This theory overcomes the limitations of traditional approaches: state, quantity, functional, and modern monetary theories. It integrates economic, social, and political aspects into a single approach. To explore the role of money in society, the work analyzes the power structures of capitalism and socialism, and examines a model of a mixed planned-market economy with a natural unconditional basic income and continuous democracy. Special attention is paid to the two-dimensional nature of power and its convertibility through money, which opens up new perspectives for the study of economic and social systems. This work is addressed to economists, sociologists, political scientists, and anyone interested in issues of power, exchange, and money in modern society.

title: The Political Economy of Regenerative Capital: Incentives, Power, and Institutional Behaviour under Perpetual Social Capital

detail.title: The Political Economy of Regenerative Capital: Incentives, Power, and Institutional Behaviour under Perpetual Social Capital

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial, personal, or institutional conflicts of interest related to this research. The analysis and conclusions presented are solely the author’s own academic work and were not influenced by any external party.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants, patient data, or clinical interventions and therefore did not require ethics committee approval. No identifiable personal data were collected or analysed.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The work was independently conducted and funded by the author without support from any institution, grantmaker, or organisation.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines how Perpetual Social Capital (PSC)—defined as zero-interest, non-liability, soft-repayable, and indefinitely recyclable capital—reshapes political and institutional incentives across public-good systems. Whereas prior work has formalised PSC as a fourth capital class distinct from debt, equity, and grants, its political economy implications remain undertheorised. Using a public-choice and institutional economics framework, the paper analyses how PSC reallocates capital power, attenuates fragility-based control mechanisms, reduces donor and treasury discretion, and enhances autonomy for frontline institutions.

PSC eliminates leverage and interest extraction, breaks the single-cycle dependency inherent in grant structures, and introduces multi-cycle regenerative capital flows that weaken the political authority typically exercised through scarcity. The paper shows how PSC alters the behaviour of bureaucracies, modifies donor psychology, disrupts gatekeeping dynamics, crowds in long-horizon public investment, and facilitates institutional planning across decades.

We argue that PSC functions not only as a financial innovation but as a governance technology: it restructures the incentive landscape of public-good provision, reduces systemic fragility, and induces a new political equilibrium characterised by stability, decentralisation, and cooperative capital governance. The conclusion situates PSC as a mechanism with inherently political effects, altering the authority structures that govern public-good systems and redefining the relationship between capital, power, and institutional autonomy.

title: Escalation Dynamics in Global AI Investment
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Division of Science and Mathmatics

detail.title: Escalation Dynamics in Global AI Investment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This article does not contain any studies with human participants or animals performed by any of the authors, and therefore, no ethical approval was required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: The global pursuit of Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) presents a profound socio-technical paradox: resource allocation, measured in hundreds of billions of dollars, is driven by belief in AGI's inevitability rather than compelling empirical evidence. This paper dissects the cognitive and institutional mechanisms sustaining this persistent, supra-rational investment. We analyze this phenomenon through three interconnected theoretical lenses. First, micro-level investment decisions are modeled as an escalating Dollar Auction Game, intensified by the psychological dynamics of Escalation of Commitment, forcing actors to defend sunk costs rather than maximize rational gains. Second, this irrational trajectory is institutionally validated through organizational Sense-making (where colossal capital expenditure is used to manufacture plausibility) and shielded by Pluralistic Ignorance, which suppresses internal dissent and fabricates a false consensus on technical feasibility. This cycle creates a powerful, self-justifying lock-in, where the financial and political fear of not competing outweighs the rational assessment of technical risk. We conclude by highlighting the critical gap between the manufactured institutional consensus and the necessary skepticism voiced by technical and ethical experts, arguing that this mechanism drives measurable geopolitical conflict escalation.

title: An Algebraic Characterization of Arbitrage-Free Pricing in Finite Asset Markets
affiliations: Independent researcher

detail.title: An Algebraic Characterization of Arbitrage-Free Pricing in Finite Asset Markets
detail.abstract: We study a finite one-period asset market using only finite-dimensional linear algebra. Assets are represented by payoff vectors in R n , trading strategies by vectors in R d , and attainable payoffs by the image of a linear map. Arbitrage is expressed as the intersection of a linear subspace with a convex cone in R×R n. We prove that the absence of arbitrage is equivalent to the existence of a strictly positive state-price vector q ∈ R n such that p = A ⊤ q. The proof is purely algebraic and relies on separation of convex sets and dual cones. We also discuss redundant assets, the induced linear relations among prices, and a simple term-structure application.
